10805-count-the-cost-an-address-to-the-p:
Writing as Jonathan Steadfast, an author addressed the people of Connecticut in Count the Cost in 1804, on sundry political subjects and a proposed new constitution. The pamphlet opens with Washington's Farewell Address warning against combinations that lift ambitious men to unjust dominion. Its title asks, with Luke, who builds a tower without first counting the cost.

The address urges voters to weigh change carefully, lest popular ends serve cunning men. Its tone is Federalist and cautionary, rooted in the early republic's debates. Readers get a sharp period pamphlet on constitutions, parties, and the price of rash reform.
15437-the-letters-of-lord-nelson-to-lady:
This second volume, printed in London in 1814, gathers Admiral Lord Nelson's letters to Lady Hamilton, numbered from forty onward. It continues a correspondence that mixes naval business, affection, and the daily news of war. The letters were published after Nelson's death, when public interest in the admiral and his famous lover ran high.

A supplement adds letters of wider interest. Nelson writes to his adopted daughter Horatia and to Charlotte Nelson. Letters from Alexander Davison to Lady Hamilton, and from Sir William Hamilton to his wife, follow. Together they sketch a circle of family, friends, and patrons around a national hero. Readers get Nelson in his own voice, warm, hurried, and direct, rather than in a formal biography.
23286-the-rover-boys-under-canvas-or-the:
Arthur M. Winfield, the pen name of Edward Stratemeyer, wrote this Rover Boys adventure, published in New York with pictures. The boys camp under canvas and stumble on the mystery of a wrecked submarine, a prize that draws rivals and danger.

A frontispiece cry of wonder marks their first sight of the wreck. The novel mixes camp life, boating, and detective work in Stratemeyer's brisk style, and it kept the long-running series fresh for a new set of boy readers. Stratemeyer keeps camp life, boating, and detection moving at a brisk pace. Before the submarine mystery, the boys play baseball, survive ammunition factory explosions, and stage a rescue on the lake.
33210-the-frontier-boys-in-the-grand-can:
Capt. Wyn Roosevelt's boys' adventure sends the Frontier Boys into the Grand Canyon in search of treasure. Copyrighted in 1908, its chapters move from a race and a chase after antelope to a fort, a captain's scheme, a mountain fire, and a mesa village. The boys build a boat, take to the river, and face an ambush on the Colorado, with a visitor and a guide named Juarez adding to the peril.

Roosevelt writes for young readers who love the outdoors, with brave lads, clear dangers, and a wild land as the true test. The canyon itself looms large, in river, mesa, and night camp. For fans of frontier tales, the book is a brisk, old-fashioned adventure, full of river work, narrow escapes, and the lure of hidden treasure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-le-bo:
French theologian Jacques Le Bossu was born at Paris in 1546. He died at Rome in 1626. He was a doctor of the Sorbonne. He entered the Benedictine order at the royal abbey of St Denis. There he became claustral prior. He tutored Cardinal de Guise. He took a prominent part in the Catholic League.

He also took part in disputes over Henry III's successor. He viewed Henry III's death as just punishment. Henry IV's accession, and Guise's execution in 1587, forced him from France in 1591. He went to Rome and entered curial service. He became consultor of the Congregatio de Auxiliis, set up in 1599 to settle the grace dispute between Dominicans and Jesuits. After its dissolution in 1607, he wished to return to France. Pope Paul V kept him at Rome. His chief work attacked twenty-five propositions of Molina.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prefecture-ap:
This prefecture was split off the Northern Kan-su mission in 1905 for the Belgian Congregation of the Immaculate Heart of Mary, of Scheutveld, Brussels. It holds the seven south prefectures of Kan-su: Tsin-chou, Ping-liang-fu, Kung-chang-fu, King-chou, Kiai-chou, King-yang-fu, and Kung-yuen-fu. Its folk number about 8,000,000. Reverend Everard Joseph Terlaak of Tsin-chou is the mission's first prefect apostolic.

In 1907 the mission counted 1 prefect apostolic, 10 missionaries, and 3 native priests. It held 23 churches and chapels, 6 schools with 42 pupils, 1 college with 5 pupils, 3 orphan asylums with 35 children, and 1,031 Catholics. In 1908 it counted 1 prefect apostolic, 12 missionaries, 3 native priests, and 1,106 Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-a-jesu:
Thomas a Jesu, born Diaz Sanchez de Avila at Baeza in 1564, became a Discalced Carmelite and a writer on mystical theology. He studied humanities, divinity and law at Salamanca before joining the Carmelites at Valladolid in 1586. Later posts took him to Seville, Saragossa and Old Castile, and he shaped a way of life for small desert houses where friars could live as hermits for a set time.

His writings on prayer and the spiritual life drew wide notice, and he pressed for a missionary branch of the order, the Congregation of St. Paul, founded in 1608. He also set up convents across the Low Countries and argued, in works of 1610 and 1613, for a central mission office of the kind later created as Propaganda. The entry closes with a companion life of Dominic a Jesu Maria, who carried the same missionary work to Vienna and beyond.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicariate-apo:
Northern Kan-su is a Chinese vicariate taking in Kuku-nor, northern Tibet. The five northern prefectures of Kan-su province, Lan-chou, Si-ning, Liang-chou, Kan-chou, and Su-chou. Its peoples include Chinese, Turkestan Turks, Mongols, and Tanguts, some eight million souls among whom there were only 2,700 Catholics, under Mgr Ubert Otto, resident at Sung-shu-chang-tsz.

Kan-su belonged to the Shen-si vicariate from 1844 until 1878, when it was erected separately and entrusted to Belgium's Congregation of the Immaculate Heart of Mary at Scheut. Later slices were carved away: Ning-hia to South-Western Mongolia in 1886, Sin-kiang as an independent mission in 1888, and seven southern prefectures as a prefecture in 1905. In 1907 the mission had a bishop, eighteen priests, twenty-four churches and chapels, schools, a college, and orphan asylums.
count-the-cost-an-address-to-the-people-:
A political address to the people of Connecticut, signed Jonathan Steadfast and dated 1804, urges them to count the cost of a new state constitution. David Daggett stands behind the pen name in the record for this tract. A line from Washington's Farewell Address warns against factions on the title page.

The writer takes his text from the verse about a man who builds a tower. He argues that great changes should not be tried till their gains and harms are weighed. Charges that the present rulers act without right, and talk of tyranny, are met head on. The piece is a sharp sample of early American debate over how a state should be ruled.
doe-osti-17047519-critical-minerals-use-:
Seminar slide deck from April 22, 2026, led by Sherif Khalifa with Sam Reese, Tapajyoti Ghosh, Julien Walzberg, and Alberta Carpenter, tracks critical minerals inside data centers. Data centers used about 4.4 percent of United States electricity in 2023, a share projected to reach 12 percent by 2028 in the cited Berkeley Lab study. Growth is driven by AI servers and hyperscale sites.

Using Berkeley Lab deployment scenarios, the team sized demand for copper, neodymium, dysprosium, and gallium in computing gear. Power and cooling hardware add much more copper and aluminum demand on top. Later slides cover supply chains, life cycle effects, and recycling paths, called circularity, for these materials.
doe-osti-17134355-critical-minerals-use-:
Sherif Khalifa, Sam Reese, Tapajyoti Ghosh, and colleagues presented on critical minerals in data centers at an April 2026 seminar in the AMMTO Innovation Impact series. Data centers were estimated by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory to use 4.4 percent of United States electricity in 2023, rising toward 12 percent by 2028. Growth driven by AI also strains mineral supply, the talk argues.

Using Berkeley deployment scenarios, the team quantified demand for copper, neodymium, dysprosium, and gallium in computing gear. Power and cooling infrastructure adds heavy demand for copper, aluminum, and power electronics. Slides trace minerals from component level intensity to sector wide totals, then turn to lifecycle and circularity options for easing the strain on supply chains.
doe-osti-2589842-geant4-simulations-and-:
Lauren Mendoza, Alexander Leder, and James Harding support a neutrino telescope planned for the Pacific Ocean, in Los Alamos report LA-UR-25-29584, issued 26 September 2025. The Pacific Ocean Neutrino Experiment, P-ONE, will hang light sensors deep in the sea to catch flashes from passing neutrinos. Reading those flashes right depends on knowing how light scatters in seawater.

The team modeled detector response with the Geant4 toolkit and compared it with bench experiments on light sensors. One bench fix cut a resistor from 47 megohms to 10 kilohms so the sensor could handle brighter light without saturating. Scattering values for the Mie model, which describes light bouncing off particles in the water, are still estimates. Better water values may shift the symmetry the simulations now show.
doe-osti-3005953-pulsed-neutron-die-away:
Pulsed-neutron die-away measurements on water targets, run at Lawrence Livermore in October 2023, are documented here as a formal benchmark (LLNL-TR-2003024). Evaluator Ruby Araj, with internal reviewer Daniel Siefman and independent reviewers Jesse Holmes and Adam Ney, describes a deuterium-tritium generator firing 14.1 MeV neutron pulses into water targets of several sizes. Helium-3 detectors around each target record how the neutron count fades with time, and the decay gives a time eigenvalue, alpha, for each case.

The benchmark exists to test thermal neutron scattering laws for water. Four target cases carry full uncertainty budgets for alpha, broken down by target height, diameter, temperature, and density. Models built in MCNP6.2 with ENDF/B-VIII.0 data use listed simplifications, such as dropping electronics and detector holders. A cross-check with the MC21 code matched the MCNP eigenvalues closely for all four cases.
doe-osti-3009705-s-amp-tr-oct-nov-2025-r:
The October/November 2025 issue of Science and Technology Review, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's magazine, is its Research SLAM issue. Writers Lilly Ackerman and Elliot Jaffe are among the contributors, with Suzanne Storar as publication editor.

The cover feature follows the laboratory's annual Research SLAM, where postdoctoral researchers get three minutes and one slide to explain complex work to a nontechnical audience, with winners advancing to national competition. Research highlights cover liquids confined in the world's smallest water channels and a new approach to treating fentanyl overdose. The issue also carries a remembrance of Johnny Foster and a commentary by Patricia Falcone.
doe-osti-3011525-strong-a-multi-sensor-a:
Bird and bat collisions with offshore wind turbines are measured with a multi sensor system in a final report prepared by WEST Inc of Cheyenne, Wyoming. The Netherlands Organisation for Applied Scientific Research contributed to the work. The cooperative agreement DE-EE0008734 ran from November 2019 to December 2024 under the Wind Energy Technologies Office. Land based fatality counting relies on carcass searches, which cannot work at sea.

Four thermal camera stations stood one to two metres from a turbine base, aimed up at the nacelle. The Axis cameras recorded ten second clips at 640 by 480 resolution and 30 frames per second. Colour cameras supplemented two stations. Rhett Good and Jennifer Stucker led the prime recipient team.
doe-osti-3012801-assessment-of-sup-180-1:
Lawrence Livermore report LLNL-TR-2014652, by A. P. Tonchev, S. Quaglioni, and K. Kravvaris, dated December 11, 2025, assesses photonuclear data for five tungsten isotopes: 180, 182, 183, 184, and 186. When electron beams stop in tungsten, a common converter material in research and medical accelerators, they produce bremsstrahlung photons. Those photons can knock neutrons out of nuclei, and planners need reliable rates for that reaction.

The authors gathered the experimental record from the EXFOR database and older literature, then scored each evaluated data library against it with a new tool called CEREAL. For isotope 180 they found no direct experimental cross-section data at all. The assessment shows where the libraries agree with measurement and where they rest on little or no evidence.

doe-osti-3363293-steam-generators-therma: Nuclear plants make steam to spin turbines, and the steam generators are where heat becomes power. This report covers the instruments and measurements that track water flow and heat inside them. Good measurements keep these giant machines safe and running at full strength.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WDSU_WDSU: WDSU, another broadcast call sign, is the whole title of this declassified US government file. The Internet Archive's entry adds nothing - no year, no subject note. Text unlocated publicly. Call letters in the government files.
nasa-tm-19660026616-high-vacuum-technolo:
Engineers and scientists gathered at NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, Ohio, on June 8 and 9, 1965, to compare notes on vacuum technology. This volume collects the papers they presented. The shared problem was practical: how to build chambers on Earth that copy the near-empty conditions of space.

The contents cover simulation facilities, testing methods, and measurement tools. Papers describe a cryogenic quartz crystal microbalance, an ultrahigh vacuum research facility, and a very large unbaked vacuum system. Others treat launch simulation and a vacuum system for liquid-metal heat transfer work. Together the papers record the state of vacuum testing in the mid-1960s.
nasa-tm-19680014726-electric-fields-in-s:
William I. Linlor examines electric fields in space and on the lunar surface in this NASA paper. Together with magnetic fields, electric fields push plasma along drift paths. Strong fields could even propel vehicles without spending fuel, like sunlight pushing on reflecting vanes.

Most theorists of the time assumed space electric fields are near zero. Linlor notes that no experiment had yet verified that claim. He argues that theory needs a firm base of real measurements first. The paper then describes a sensitive measuring system built for that job. Its data, he stresses, must be clear enough that no one can misread what they mean.
nasa-tm-19690012796-a-mass-spectrometric:
Atomic oxygen dominates the upper atmosphere, yet it resists direct measurement because it reacts on nearly every surface it touches. A NASA technique described here turns that weakness into the method itself. Mass spectrometers flew on the Geoprobe rocket and the Explorer 32 satellite, breathing air through knife-edged openings into their ion sources.

Silver oxide coatings inside the sources rejoined atomic oxygen into molecular oxygen, which the instruments could count. High above Earth, that count yields the atomic oxygen density outside. The data brought cautions, the authors report. Surface joining proved far weaker than expected, so readings give good lower limits only. Bench results at higher pressures, they add, cannot be stretched to space conditions.
nasa-tm-19710024215-performance-of-a-dir:
James E Vrancik of the Lewis Research Center tested a direct current power supply in this August 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-2349. The supply served the Brayton cycle power system, sized from two to fifteen kilowatts. It was a transformer and rectifier set feeding a twenty eight volt bus. A second output charged batteries at about forty two volts, and top output reached fourteen hundred watts.

Vrancik ran the supply across ranges of input voltage, frequency, and output current. Efficiency reached eighty nine percent at the design point. Output voltage tracked the input in a near straight line, with load regulation of six percent. He judged the overall performance satisfactory for the system.
nasa-tm-19720008738-creep-rupture-tests-:
Klaus H Gumto and Barry Weiss of the Lewis Research Center burst tested hot metal tubes for this February 1972 memorandum, NASA TM X-2505. The tubes were weld drawn Rene 41, a nickel alloy built for jet engine heat. Each tube was pressurized inside with helium gas. Then it was held at high temperature until it failed. Such creep rupture tests reveal how long hot pressure parts can serve.

The tubes were slim, under a centimeter across, with thin walls. Test heat ranged across a span near two thousand degrees Fahrenheit. Internal pressure also ranged widely between runs. Lifetimes stretched from a few hours to over two thousand hours. The spread showed how strongly heat and pressure govern failure. Designers use such curves to set safe service limits.
nasa-tm-19720015290-experimental-heat-tr:
James W Gauntner, Jan M Lane, Robert P Dengler, and Robert O Hickel reported these engine tests in April 1972, as NASA TM X-2472. The team came from the Lewis Research Center and the Army Air Mobility laboratory. Their test piece was a turbine vane with lengthwise fins. Three cooling schemes worked together inside it. Air jets struck the inner walls, a film coated the outside, and passages carried heat away.

The vane ran in a turbojet engine at full working heat. Inlet gas reached twenty five hundred degrees Fahrenheit. Coolant conditions and flow share also spanned wide ranges. The report presents the measured heat transfer and flow results. It also gives methods for matching such data into useful patterns.
podcast-joerogan-R6xHjdF4jSU:
Engineer Christopher Dunn joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2142 to argue that ancient Egypt used advanced technology. Dunn worked in manufacturing and studied the Great Pyramid as a machine part, measuring stonework with a machinist's eye. His books claim the pyramid was a power plant.

He lays out the fits, cuts, and alignments he says hand tools cannot explain. Rogan asks what mainstream Egypt experts say back, and where Dunn's proof is thinnest. The episode is the ancient-tech case in its most technical form, from a guest who speaks in tolerances rather than legends.
podcast-joerogan-g9ZU-SvOiSU:
A professor of religion gives her take on the UFO phenomenon in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. The guest reads saucers through the lens of faith, asking what belief itself reveals about the people who report visitors. It is the scholarly angle the show books once in a while.

She argues that UFO reports behave like religious experiences across history, with the same awe, fear, and life-changing weight. Rogan asks where that leaves the nuts-and-bolts question of craft in the sky. The segment suits listeners who want the meaning of the phenomenon, not just its footage, examined by someone trained to study belief.
podcast-tuckercarlson-EXPTKcLRqSU:
British politician and broadcaster George Galloway speaks to Tucker Carlson about being driven into exile. Galloway says his fierce criticism of the Ukraine war brought official pressure that pushed him out of normal public life. He presents his stand as defiance, not retreat.

Galloway recounts the steps he says were taken against him, from banking trouble to airport stops. He defends his antiwar record across decades of British politics. Carlson compares his treatment to the pressure faced by dissenters in America. Free-speech minded viewers get a famous firebrand explaining exile for words.
the-letters-of-lord-nelson-to-lady-hamil: Lord Nelson letters to Lady Hamilton fill two volumes, printed in London in 1814, and this record holds volume two. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here, listing letters numbered forty onward with their page numbers. A supplement of letters by distinguished characters is promised on the title page as well. The letters themselves, from the last years of Nelson life and command, are absent from this record.
